exampleAnswers.title: Constructing a Recursive Formula for a Geometric Sequence

question.text: What is the recursive formula for the following geometric sequence? \[ 20, \: 15, \: \dfrac{45}{4}, \: \ldots \]
question.explanation:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio $r$ takes the form \[ a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_{n}. \]

In this case, the first term is $a_1=20,$ and we can calculate the common ratio $r$ as

\[ r=\dfrac{a_2}{a_1}=\dfrac{15}{20}=\dfrac{3}{4}.\]

Consequently, the recursive formula for this sequence is

\[ a_{n+1} = \dfrac{3}{4}\,a_{n}, \quad a_{1}=20,\quad n\geq 1. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given Its Recursive Formula

question.text: What is the $4$th term of the geometric sequence given below? \[a_{n+1} =-\dfrac{1}{2} a_n,\qquad a_1 = 128,\qquad n\geq 1\]
question.explanation: We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term: \[ \begin{align} a_1 &= 128\\[5pt] a_2 &= -\dfrac{1}{2} a_1 =-\dfrac{1}{2}(128) = -64\\[5pt] a_3 &= -\dfrac{1}{2} a_2 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(-64) = 32 \\[5pt] a_4 &=-\dfrac{1}{2} a_3 =-\dfrac{1}{2}(32)= -16 \end{align} \] Therefore, $a_4=-16.$

example.title: Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given Its Recursive Formula

question.text:
Consider the following geometric sequence:
\[
a_{n+1} =\dfrac14 a_n,\qquad a_1 = 256,\qquad n\geq 1
\]
question.explanation:
We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term: \begin{align} a_1 &= 256\\[5pt] a_2 &= \dfrac{1}{4} a_1 =\dfrac{1}{4}(256) = 64\\[5pt] a_3 &= \dfrac{1}{4} a_2 = \dfrac{1}{4}(64) = 16 \\[5pt] a_4 &=\dfrac{1}{4} a_3 =\dfrac{1}{4}(16)= 4 \end{align}

Therefore, $a_4=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{4}.$

question.text: What is the $3$rd term of the geometric sequence given below? \[a_{n+1} =-5 a_n,\qquad a_1 = \dfrac{1}{75},\qquad n\geq 1\]
question.explanation: We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $3$rd term: \[ \begin{align} a_1 &= \dfrac{1}{75}\\[5pt] a_2 &= -5a_1 =-5\left(\dfrac{1}{75}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{15}\\[5pt] a_3 &= -5a_2 =-5\left(-\dfrac{1}{15}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3} \end{align} \] Therefore, $a_3=\dfrac{1}{3}.$

\]

Therefore, $a_3=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{12}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given a Recursive Formula in Function Notation

question.text:
What is the $4$th term of the geometric sequence given below?

\[ f(n+1) = -3.5f(n),\quad f(1) = -2,\quad n\geq 1 \]
question.explanation: We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term: \[ \begin{align} f(1) &= -2\\[5pt] f(2) &=-3.5 f(1) = -3.5(-2) = 7\\[5pt] f(3) &=-3.5f(2) = -3.5(7) = -24.5 \\[5pt] f(4) &=-3.5f(3) =-3.5(-24.5)= 85.75 \end{align} \] Therefore, $f(4)=85.75.$

example.title: Calculating a Term of a Geometric Sequence Given a Recursive Formula in Function Notation

question.text:
Consider the following geometric sequence:
\[
f(n+1) = \dfrac27f(n),\qquad f(1) = 343, \qquad n\geq 1
\]
question.explanation:
We use the recursive formula to compute the terms of the sequence up to the $4$th term: \begin{align*} f(1) &=343 \\[5pt] f(2) &= \dfrac27 f(1) = \dfrac27(343) = 98 \\[5pt] f(3) &= \dfrac27 f(2) = \dfrac27(98) = 28 \\[5pt] f(4) &= \dfrac27 f(3) = \dfrac27(28)= 8 \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(4)=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{8}.$

question.text:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

  1. $\dfrac{1}{3}, \: -\dfrac{4}{3}, \: -\dfrac{16}{3}, \: \dots$
  2. $-5, \: -20, \: 80, \: \dots$
  3. $f(n+1) = 4f(n)-4,\quad f(1) = 2,\quad n\geq 1$
question.explanation:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

  • Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term: \begin{align*} \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} & = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)} = -4 \\[5pt] \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} & = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{16}{3}\right)}{\left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\right)} = 4 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

  • Sequence II is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term: \begin{align*} \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} & = \dfrac{-20}{-5} = 4\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} & = \dfrac{80}{-20} = -4 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

  • Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms: \begin{align*} f(1) &=2 \\[5pt] f(2) &= 4\cdot 2 - 4 = 4 \\[5pt] f(3) &= 4\cdot 4 - 4 = 12 \end{align*} So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios: \begin{align*} \dfrac{f(2)}{f(1)} & =\dfrac{4}{2} = 2\\[5pt] \dfrac{f(3)}{f(2)} & =\dfrac{12}{4} = 3 \end{align*}

In conclusion, none of the given is a geometric sequence.

question.text:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

  1. $\dfrac 32,\:\dfrac 12,\:\dfrac 16,\: \dots$
  2. $a_{n+1} = a_n + a_n^2,\quad a_1 = 2,\quad n\geq 1$
  3. $f(n+1) = 5f(n)+ 3,\quad f(1) = \dfrac 15,\quad n\geq 1$
question.explanation:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

  • Sequence I could be a geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same: \begin{align*} \dfrac{\left( \dfrac 12 \right)}{\left( \dfrac 32 \right)} &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\[5pt] \dfrac{\left( \dfrac 16 \right)}{\left( \dfrac 12 \right)} &= \dfrac{1}{3}\\[5pt] \end{align*}

  • Sequence II is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms: \begin{align*} a_1 &=2\\[5pt] a_2 &= 2+ 2^2= 6\\[5pt] a_3 &= 6 + 6^2 =42 \end{align*} So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios: \begin{align*} \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} =\dfrac{6}{2} &= 3\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} =\dfrac{42}{6} &= 7\\[5pt] \end{align*}

  • Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms: \begin{align*} f(1) &=\dfrac 15 \\[5pt] f(2) &= 5\left( \dfrac 15 \right) + 3 = 4 \\[5pt] f(3) &= 5(4) + 3 = 23 \end{align*} So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios: \begin{align*} \dfrac{f(2)}{f(1)} &=\dfrac{4}{\left( \dfrac 15 \right)} = 20\\[5pt] \dfrac{f(3)}{f(2)} &=\dfrac{23}{4} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

In conclusion, only I is a geometric sequence.
